because: Under the Arbois cahier des charges, vin jaune stays in oak without topping up until 15 December of the sixth year after the harvest, with at least 60 months of that under voile. The examiner's other point, that "six years" says nothing about the voile, would apply just as much to every accept entry they propose to keep ("six years and three months", "6 years 3 months", "75 months"). claim: The wines may not be sold until eighteen months have passed
because: The AOC Alsace cahier des charges (INAO, section on élevage and mise en marché) does not set a period in months. It requires VT and SGN wines to be aged at least until 1 June of the second year after the harvest, and they may reach consumers only from that date. For an October harvest that is about 20 months, not a flat eighteen. The keyed option, 'About eighteen months', is still the closest choice, so the key stands. The explanation, though, states a rule the law does not contain.
fix: The wines must be aged at least until 1 June of the second year after the harvest and may not reach consumers before that date, which is roughly eighteen to twenty months. Both categories must also pass an official tasting before the term is granted.
verifyReason: The examiner says the cahier des charges "does not set a period in months". That is false. The source the examiner cites, the AOC Alsace cahier des charges (INAO PNOCDCAlsace.pdf), states the rule in months itself. Its terroir section says these wines "doivent respecter un élevage minimum de 18 mois". Elsewhere it sets the exact date: élevage "au moins jusqu'au 1er juin de la 2ème année qui suit celle de la récolte", and release "à destination du consommateur à partir du 1er juin de la 2ème année". Eighteen months is therefore the legal text's own summary of that date rule. At most it is an approximation of roughly 18 to 20 months, and the question itself asks "roughly". The keyed answer is right, and the explanation says nothing false. Calling it a flat eighteen months is a quibble, not a wrong fact.

claim: Madeira lies some seven hundred kilometres off the coast of Morocco and close to a thousand from Lisbon

verifyReason: The claim is only that the explanation's "some seven hundred kilometres" is wrong. Wikipedia does give 520 km to the African coast. Published figures disagree widely, though: search results show 520, 560, 600 and 700 km, depending on which points are measured. I computed great-circle distances from Funchal (32.65N, 16.91W). To Tarfaya, the nearest point of Morocco proper, it is about 650 km. To Cap Ghir it is about 700 km, and to Essaouira about 685 km. Even from Porto Santo, the nearest the main islands come to Morocco is about 650 km. The 520 km figure seems to count the outlying Selvagens, or to be loose. So "some seven hundred kilometres" is a fair round figure for Madeira Island, and arguably closer than 520 km. The examiner also says the Lisbon figure (close to a thousand km) and the key (Madeira) are correct. The explanation's real point, an isolated oceanic island unlike the three Mediterranean options, stands either way. At most this is a quibble over an approximate distance, not a false fact.
finalFix: No change: keep "Madeira lies some seven hundred kilometres off the coast of Morocco and close to a thousand from Lisbon".

It describes Cantemerle's 1856 entry as either an oversight or an afterthought, and calls the Dubignon removal a less known "change" in quotation marks, because that estate was absorbed into Malescot St-Exupéry and never reclassified. Trade guides (Vinfolio, FINE+RARE) note that Cantemerle's 1856 addition is often overlooked. Search summaries built on these guides call it a correction to the original list, and call Mouton's promotion the only substantive reclassification.

The explanation says "the only substantive change", not "the only change". That qualifier is the standard framing and it holds. The Cantemerle and Dubignon points are extra facts, not a false statement. A candidate who learns this line will not miss an exam answer on it, and whether Cantemerle's addition counts as "substantive" is a matter of wording, not a factual error. Under the default-to-refuted rule this does not qualify as a wrong explanation.

claim: The model answer and explanation treat 'Piesporter Michelsberg' as the current Grosslage label that misleads buyers and say it is 'still on shelves'. The German wine law reform ends that labelling.

Only older vintages still show the misleading form. A candidate sitting an exam now is expected to know this change.
